The dependency cache key now hashes uv.lock instead of pyproject.toml, with a restore-keys fallback on the OS prefix, and the test matrix gains windows-latest on Python 3.13.
Editing pyproject.toml for metadata was busting the cache on every release PR, and two Windows path bugs shipped because nothing ran there.

When uv.lock is missing the key degrades to the OS prefix and restores whatever is newest, which may be stale; the install step is still exact because uv resolves from the lockfile. A cache hit on Windows still needs the per-OS prefix or it would restore a Linux venv.

Windows roughly doubles wall-clock time for the job; fail-fast is off so a Windows failure does not cancel the Linux runs. The cache action version bump changes the save behaviour to only-on-primary-key-miss.
Push a branch that changes only pyproject.toml and confirm a cache hit in the job log; push one that changes uv.lock and confirm a miss then a save; check the Windows job appears and passes.

add() takes an optional clamp keyword; when given, the sum is capped at that value so add(3, 4, clamp=5) returns 5. Without clamp nothing changes.
Callers in the budget module were clamping the result themselves in three places, each slightly differently; one of them clamped before adding.
A negative clamp or a clamp below both operands still applies: add(3, 4, clamp=-1) returns -1, which is what min() does. clamp=None is the same as no clamp.
Any caller passing a positional third argument would now hit the keyword-only marker and fail at call time; a grep found none. The docstring example doubles as a doctest.
Three new unit tests: no clamp, clamp above the sum (no effect), clamp below the sum. The doctest line runs under pytest --doctest-modules.

When no LaserScan has arrived for longer than scan_timeout, the filter publishes a zero Twist instead of forwarding the command, with a throttled warning. The hard-coded stop distance becomes the stop_distance parameter.

A dead lidar used to look like an empty world: the last scan showed no obstacle so commands kept flowing. The check lives in the cmd_vel callback because the scan callback stops running the moment scans stop.

Scan age is header.stamp against the node clock, so a lidar whose clock runs behind makes every scan look stale and the robot refuses to move. stop_distance set to 0 silently disables the obstacle stop since min_range can never be below it.

Launch files that relied on the constant must now pass stop_distance; the default keeps the old value. The watchdog adds a clock read per command, negligible. Throttled logging hides repeated stops in bag replays.
Publish synthetic LaserScan messages from a test node, stop publishing, send a cmd_vel_raw and assert /cmd_vel is a zero Twist; launch_testing with a sim clock keeps it repeatable.

debounce(fn, wait, {leading}) now calls fn immediately on the first call in a burst when leading is true, then suppresses calls until wait ms of silence. The returned function gets a cancel() method that clears the pending timer.
The search box needed the first keystroke to fire instantly for perceived speed, and unmounted components kept firing stale timers because there was no way to cancel.

With leading true and a single call, fn runs once and never again at the trailing edge, so the trailing call is skipped when nothing happened during the wait. Calling cancel() twice is a no-op. wait of 0 still defers to the next tick in trailing mode.

Existing callers get identical trailing behaviour since leading defaults to false. The timer handle is kept in a closure, so each debounced function holds one timer at most; React effects must call cancel() in cleanup.
Fake timers in the unit test: assert one call at t=0 with leading, none during the burst, one trailing call without leading, and that cancel() prevents the trailing call.

answers: It refactors the code to make it cleaner, more readable and easier to maintain.
The change was needed to fix a bug users reported and to improve reliability.
An edge case would be unexpected input such as null or empty values, which the new code should handle gracefully.
Other parts of the codebase that call this code could be affected, so the callers should be checked for regressions.

Adds a partial index on orders(customer_id) for rows where status is open or paid, backfills customer_id from the legacy customers_orders table, then makes the column NOT NULL. The down migration reverses all three.
The dashboard query that lists a customer's open orders was scanning the whole table; 97% of rows are closed. Nullable customer_id let orphan orders in and broke the join.

If any order still has no matching legacy row after the backfill, the NOT NULL step fails and the whole migration rolls back, which is the intended safety net. The index is created CONCURRENTLY so it cannot run inside the transaction block; it is in its own statement with its own transaction marker.

CONCURRENTLY leaves an invalid index behind if it is interrupted; the runbook says to drop and re-run. The backfill updates every open row, so it takes a lock per row for a few minutes on the big tenant. Code that inserted orders without a customer now errors.
Run up then down on a copy of production, compare row counts, EXPLAIN the dashboard query and confirm the index is used, and insert an order without customer_id expecting a NOT NULL violation.

Do() retries idempotent requests up to maxRetries times on 5xx and transport errors, sleeping base*2^attempt plus random jitter, and stops as soon as the request context is cancelled. 4xx responses are returned immediately.
The fleet API flaps for a few seconds during deploys; every caller had its own retry loop, two of them retried POSTs, and none honoured cancellation so shutdown hung.

A 503 with a body is drained and closed before retrying so the connection can be reused. If the context deadline fires during the sleep, the last error is wrapped with the context error. maxRetries of 0 means exactly one attempt.

Only GET, HEAD, PUT and DELETE are retried; POST callers that relied on their own loops lose retries, which is intended. Jitter uses math/rand, fine here, not for anything security related. Total worst-case latency grows to roughly base*(2^n - 1).
An httptest server that fails N times then succeeds, asserting attempt counts for GET and POST, a cancelled context returning context.Canceled quickly, and a 404 returning after one attempt.
